column2: On the morning itself, you can take up to four days off a year, and the boss can rarely say no.
column4: Poland's 'urlop na żądanie' (leave on demand) comes out of the normal holiday allowance. You ask by the first day of leave; employers need an exceptional reason to refuse.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; courts allow refusal in rare cases, so 'rarely say no' is hedged

column2: When a public holiday lands on a Saturday, employees get another weekday off in exchange.
column4: Polish labour law counts a Saturday holiday as time already off, so the employer must grant a replacement day within the same settlement period. Freelance contracts don't get it.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; other countries may have similar compensation rules (fits guess)

column2: Pay comes in two parts: an advance in the middle of the month and the rest at the end.
column4: Ukrainian law requires pay at least twice a month, at most 16 days apart (the 'avans' and the final payment). Mexico's 'quincena' is also paid fortnightly.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; MX fit is a guess; advance/final split is practice rather than a legal term

column2: From intern to CEO, everyone is on a first-name basis.
column4: Dutch workplaces are flat and managers go by first name. American offices are informal too, but open disagreement with the boss is especially expected in the Netherlands.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; traditional Dutch firms may differ; US fit is a guess

column2: Each December, employers hand staff a Christmas hamper or a gift voucher.
column4: Dutch 'kerstpakket' (about 7.4 million employees get a pack or card); Italian 'cesto natalizio', often with panettone. Many firms now let staff pick a gift.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; Italian side backed only by commercial/blog sources (fits guess)

column2: By law, the weeks you take off come with an extra payment on top of your usual salary.
column4: Brazil's 'terço de férias' adds a third of a month's pay; Mexico's 'prima vacacional' is at least 25% of holiday pay. The Dutch 'vakantiegeld' (8%) is similar.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; NL fit is a guess (allowance not tied to taking leave); Mexican 25% figure from expansion.mx search result

column2: At year's end, colleagues pool money for one shared lottery ticket, and each person gets a receipt for their share.
column4: Brazil's 'bolão' (often for the 'Mega da Virada' draw) and the American 'office pool' work the same way: friends, family or coworkers buy shares of one bet.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; source covers the rules, not how common it is at work; US fit is a guess

column2: Some national holidays are moved to a Monday to create a long weekend.
column4: Mexico shifts Constitution Day, Juárez's birthday and Revolution Day to Mondays; in the US, Memorial Day and Presidents' Day always fall on a Monday.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; US part from general knowledge (Monday Holidays Act)

column2: The December office party shares its name with a nine-day pre-Christmas tradition and usually includes a gift swap.
column4: 'Posada' means lodging, after the pre-Christmas custom. The corporate version is a staff party with a gift exchange and recognition of the team's year.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; the name has a religious origin, text covers only the secular party; flag for review

column2: Showing loyalty to your employer is called 'putting on the company shirt'.
column4: Mexican 'ponerse la camiseta', a football image: bosses use it to ask for extra effort, and younger staff often joke about it. Brazil has a similar 'vestir a camisa'.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; Brazilian phrase not confirmed by a source (fits guess)

column2: A friendly work email that says 'per my last email' is read as a polite-sounding rebuke.
column4: It means 'I already told you'. A Preply survey ranked it the most passive-aggressive email phrase, ahead of 'friendly reminder' and 'thanks in advance'.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; commercial survey; English-speaking offices elsewhere use it too but none are in the ten

column2: Your health insurance usually comes through your job, with a short window each autumn to choose a plan.
column4: Employer plans cover about 60% of Americans. Most firms hold a two-to-four-week 'open enrollment' in the fall; miss it and you wait a year unless a life event qualifies you.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; the 60% figure is from Wikipedia, the open-enrollment timing from search summaries (Gusto/NerdWallet pages blocked)

column2: On Fridays, the dress code relaxes and jeans are fine.
column4: 'Casual Friday' grew from Hawaii's 1960s 'Aloha Friday' and spread across US offices, helped by a 1992 khakis-maker guide to casual business wear.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; dress codes are relaxed in other offices too (fits guess)

column2: Someone insists on paying for the whole group's coffee, and the others protest that it's their turn next.
column4: Italian 'offro io' (my treat): the friendly argument over the bill is part of the ritual. Turkish hosts also insist on paying.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; source covers the offer, not the rotation; may overlap tr-015; TR fit is a guess

column2: People who work a bit over the standard week earn extra days off, on top of normal paid holiday.
column4: 'RTT' (réduction du temps de travail) arrived in 2000 with the 35-hour week: hours beyond 35 are paid back as time off. Entitlement depends on the company agreement.
column10: draft v3; theme: office

column2: Outside working hours, staff have a legal right not to answer work messages.
column4: France's 'droit à la déconnexion' (since 2017) bars sanctions for ignoring messages out of hours; Italy's 'diritto alla disconnessione' covers remote work.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; legal nuance (a duty to negotiate, rarely enforced); Italian part from general knowledge, unsourced

column2: After lunch, office workers stroll back holding a takeaway iced coffee, even in winter.
column4: Iced Americano, nicknamed 'ah-ah', is Korea's unofficial national drink and outsells hot even in winter. Americans also drink iced coffee through the cold months.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; US fit is a guess

column2: A team dinner often moves on to a second venue, such as a bar or karaoke place, called the 'second round'.
column4: Hoesik (company dinner): 1-cha is the dinner, 2-cha the follow-up. Younger staff increasingly skip the later rounds.
column10: draft v3; theme: office; alcohol-adjacent, reviewer check; 'increasingly skip' comes from a news search summary

column2: Cheering before the result is in is discouraged: 'don't praise the day before sunset'.
column4: Polish 'Nie chwal dnia przed zachodem słońca', Ukrainian 'Ne khvaly dnia do vechora': the local 'don't count your chickens before they hatch'.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; Ukrainian version not sourced (fits guess)

column2: Wishing luck before an exam, you say 'neither fluff nor feather', and the answer is 'go to hell'.
column4: 'Ni pukha, ni pera!' – 'Do bisa!' Hunters feared forest spirits would spoil a hunt if they heard a wish for success, so they wished the opposite. Still said before exams.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; similar phrases may exist in neighbouring languages (fits guess); same habit type as it-026

column2: One short word means 'let's', 'come on' and, at the end of a chat or call, 'bye'.
column4: Ukrainian 'davai': 'davai pidemo' = let's go; as a farewell it's informal and interchangeable with 'buvai'.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; the 'let's' and 'come on' senses are shared with neighbouring languages (fits guess)

column2: Standing out is discouraged with a saying: the head above the field gets chopped off.
column4: 'Als je je kop boven het maaiveld uitsteekt, wordt hij eraf gehakt.' A TU Delft piece says it's often used to shrug off criticism, though it holds 'a grain of truth'.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; close in spirit to nl-021; Australian 'tall poppy' is similar but outside the ten

column2: On New Year's Eve, families watch a comedian run through the year's news in one long monologue.
column4: The 'oudejaarsconference' began with Wim Kan's radio show in 1954 and is now a TV tradition, often watched with fried dough balls.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; the genre is political satire, text avoids it; flag against the politics rule; 1954 date from a search summary

column2: There's a word for non-stop joking and teasing among friends, and it names a style of internet memes too.
column4: 'Zoeira': to tease ('zoar', 'tirar sarro') is affectionate, and being teased means you belong. Football banter and WhatsApp groups are prime territory.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; meme sense from an academic paper seen in search, not opened; teasing culture also exists elsewhere (fits guess)

column2: Taxi drivers and street sellers call you 'boss', 'chief' or 'young man' to be friendly.
column4: Mexican 'jefe', 'patrón' and 'joven'; Turkish 'şef', 'kaptan' and 'hocam' (my teacher); Brazilian 'chefe'. Friendly, never literal.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; source lists the Mexican terms only; TR and BR terms from general knowledge (fits guess)

column2: Parents announce on a car sticker that their child is on the honor roll.
column4: 'My child is an honor student at…' stickers are common enough to inspire the joke reply 'My kid beat up your honor student' (first printed in 1990).
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; fading with newer generations

column2: Offered more food or a drink you don't want, you politely say 'I'm good'.
column4: 'I'm good' has become a standard American way to decline an offer, from second helpings to a free sample.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; AI-generated, no source found; unsure whether it is distinct enough from other English-speaking habits

column2: Teenagers pepper their sentences with a filler word that literally means 'that is'.
column4: 'Cioè' means 'that is' or 'namely' but works like 'like' or 'you know'. A teen magazine is even named after it.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; 'teen magazine' fact from a search summary of the same article

column2: Asked if the film was good, a puff of breath and a shrug can be the whole answer.
column4: 'Bof' is more a sound than a word: meh, so-so. It can also answer 'ça va?' with a lukewarm 'not great'.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; Italian 'boh' is a cousin (a shrug for 'no idea'), so IT fit is possible but not added

column2: Complimented on anything, people wave it away with 'no, no, not at all'.
column4: Korean 'aniyo' (no) and Turkish 'estağfurullah' deflect praise politely. Studies suggest younger Koreans increasingly just say thanks.
column10: draft v3; theme: banter; Turkish part from tr-030 and general knowledge (fits guess); younger-generation shift from a search summary

column2: To pay online, you type a six-digit code that your banking app generates for a couple of minutes.
column4: BLIK, launched in 2015, also works in shops and ATMs and for transfers between friends by phone number.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; payment-by-phone rather than messaging, but fits the phones theme

column2: A row of closing brackets, like ')))', means a smile or a laugh.
column4: More brackets mean more amusement, while '(((' signals sadness. Heavy use can read as irony.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; the same convention is used in neighbouring chat cultures; other fits unchecked

column2: People answer the phone by saying their own name, with the word 'with' in front.
column4: 'Met Pim': a bare 'hello' can sound abrupt. Skip your name and the caller may ask 'met wie spreek ik?' (with whom am I speaking?).
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; 'rude' claim comes from one commenter, softened in the note

column2: The verb for sending a chat message is built from an app's name.
column4: 'Whatsappen' was added to a Dutch dictionary in 2012, next to 'googelen' and 'facebooken'; the short 'appen' is everyday speech.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; DutchNews covers 'whatsappen' only; 'appen' from a Wiktionary search result; text names no app, but similar verbs exist elsewhere (fits guess)

column2: A reply to a question is often a voice note of several minutes, not a text.
column4: Brazil's 'áudio' (WhatsApp's president says Brazilians send about four times more voice messages than any other country), Italian 'vocale', Turkish 'sesli mesaj'.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; MX, IT and TR fits rest on language-blog claims

column2: Asking for someone's number, people use a short nickname for the main chat app instead of its name.
column4: 'Me passa seu zap?' ('zap' or 'zap-zap' is Brazilian shorthand for WhatsApp). Zuckerberg praised Brazilians for making 'Zap Zap' their own.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; nickname confirmed in news text, the exact 'give me your zap' phrasing is my example

column2: Replying with a sticker, often homemade from a friend's face, is routine.
column4: Brazil's 'figurinhas' are often homemade; Korea's chat 'emoticons' are mostly bought character packs. Zuckerberg says Brazilians send more stickers than anyone.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; KR half rests on an Asia Times article (asiatimes.com/?p=323265); 'homemade' detail from search results only

column2: A typed laugh starts with the letter J, since the letter is pronounced like an H.
column4: 'Jajaja' is the written laugh, 'jejeje' a sly chuckle and 'jijiji' a mischievous giggle. Typing 'haha' can look like a typo.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; same convention across Spanish-speaking countries, Mexico is the only one in the ten

column2: A green message bubble in the group chat can make a teenager feel left out.
column4: iMessage shows iPhone-to-iPhone texts in blue and others in green. With about 87% of US teens on iPhones (Piper Sandler), the colour became a status marker.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; data from 2021-22, Android RCS may be softening it

column2: In messages, 'okay' shrinks to a three-consonant skeleton.
column4: 'Tamam' becomes 'tmm', 'selam' 'slm' and 'ne haber' 'nbr'. Texters also drop the soft ğ, so 'sağol' turns into 'saol'.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; 'saol' detail from a search summary

column2: Phones are answered with a polite word that literally means 'my lord'.
column4: 'Efendim?' is the respectful pickup (also a polite 'pardon?'); 'alo' is the casual one, and many people use both.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; native forums disagree on efendim versus alo; same idea as mx-023 'mande' in spirit

column2: Phones are answered with the word for 'ready'.
column4: 'Pronto?' dates from manual switchboards, when the operator said the line was ready. The fuller form is 'Pronto, chi parla?' (who's speaking?).
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; origin theories differ (switchboard versus military habit)

column2: Arriving outside, you give a friend a missed call: one ring, then hang up.
column4: Italian 'fare uno squillo' (to make a ring) was a way to save credit when calls were costly. The same trick exists in other countries.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; fading as calls became free; BR, TR and MX fits from general knowledge

column2: Laughing in a text is typed as three letters standing for 'died of laughter'.
column4: 'mdr' (mort de rire); 'ptdr' (pété de rire) is the stronger version. People type it but rarely say it aloud.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; 'ptdr' strength is disputed between sources

column2: Nearly everyone uses the same chat app, which also handles work chats, shopping and gift-giving.
column4: KakaoTalk is used by about 90% of smartphone owners; its gift service lets you send a voucher or parcel to a friend straight from a chat.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; gift-service detail from a Business of Fashion search result (page blocked)

column2: A small number beside your chat message shows how many people haven't read it yet, and it vanishes once they do.
column4: KakaoTalk counts unread readers (a '1') instead of showing read ticks, so in a group chat the number counts down.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; source is a Japanese lifestyle blog

column2: In chats, 'yes' is typed as two round letters, and 'thanks' as just its first two consonants.
column4: ㅇㅇ (from 응응) means yes, ㄱㅅ (from 감사) means thanks and ㅇㅋ means okay. Very casual, among friends.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; laughing as ㅋㅋㅋ is excluded as it already exists

column2: Phones are answered with a phrase that literally means 'look here'.
column4: 'Yeoboseyo' is usually explained as 'yeogi boseyo' (look here). It's the standard phone greeting but sounds unprofessional in business calls.
column10: draft v3; theme: messaging; etymology rests on learner guides, not a linguistic source
